result:
This is the design I'd ship: tenant-scoped bearer tokens, flat document IDs, cursor pagination, a major version in the path, and RFC 9457 errors.

```
GET  POST                /v1/collections
GET  PATCH DELETE        /v1/collections/{collection_id}
GET  POST                /v1/collections/{collection_id}/documents
GET  PUT PATCH DELETE    /v1/documents/{document_id}
GET                      /v1/documents/{document_id}/revisions
GET                      /v1/documents/{document_id}/revisions/{revision}
```

```json
{
  "id": "doc_8fK2pQ",
  "collection_id": "col_31xZ",
  "revision": 7,
  "created_at": "2026-10-08T12:00:00Z",
  "updated_at": "2026-10-08T12:04:10Z",
  "content": { "any": "JSON" }
}
```

**Resources.** The tenant never appears in the URL; it comes from the credential. That way there is no path-versus-token mismatch check to forget, which is the usual source of cross-tenant leaks. Every query filters by the token's tenant, and an ID belonging to another tenant returns 404 rather than 403, so existence does not leak. Documents are created and listed under a collection but addressed flat by ID, so moving one is a `PATCH` of `collection_id` and its URL stays the same. User content sits under `content`, so system fields can be added without colliding with user keys.

**Writes.** Every write creates an immutable revision. `GET` returns an `ETag`, and `PUT`, `PATCH` and `DELETE` require `If-Match`, returning 428 if it is missing and 412 if it is stale, so concurrent editors cannot silently overwrite each other. `POST` accepts an `Idempotency-Key` header so clients can retry creates safely.

**Auth.** Clients send `Authorization: Bearer <token>`. Users get short-lived OAuth2/OIDC access tokens and services get API keys. Both resolve server-side to the same triple: one tenant, one principal, and scopes such as `documents:read` and `documents:write`. A token is bound to exactly one tenant, so a user in two tenants holds two tokens. Rate limits are per tenant and return 429 with `Retry-After`.

**Pagination.** Lists use an opaque cursor: `GET ...?limit=50&cursor=...` returns `{"data": [...], "next_cursor": "..."}`, with `null` on the last page. The cursor is a keyset on `(created_at, id)`, so pages stay stable under concurrent inserts and cost the same at any depth, where offset pagination skips or repeats rows and slows down. The limit defaults to 50 and caps at 200. There is no total count, because it is expensive at scale. The cursor encodes the filters and sort, so changing them mid-iteration returns 400.

**Versioning.** The major version lives in the path because it is visible in logs and trivial to route. Additive changes (new fields, new endpoints, new optional parameters) ship inside `/v1`, and clients must ignore unknown fields. Breaking changes go to `/v2`, with `Deprecation` and `Sunset` headers on `/v1` for a published window. API versions are unrelated to document revisions.

**Errors.** Every error is `application/problem+json` (RFC 9457) with two extensions: a stable machine-readable `code` and a `request_id` for support.

```json
{
  "type": "https://api.example.com/errors/validation-failed",
  "title": "Validation failed",
  "status": 422,
  "code": "validation_failed",
  "detail": "The request body has 1 invalid field.",
  "request_id": "req_7Hq2",
  "errors": [{ "pointer": "/content/title", "detail": "must be a string" }]
}
```

Clients branch on `code` and never on `detail`. The statuses used are 400 (malformed), 401 (no or bad token), 403 (missing scope), 404 (absent or other tenant), 409 (conflict), 412 and 428 (preconditions), 413 (content over the size cap), 422 (validation) and 429 (rate limit).

I left out search, bulk operations, binary attachments, per-document ACLs and tenant administration. Each is a separate surface that can be added later without changing anything above.
